name: Kulintangan
description: A graduated set of small bossed pot gongs that forms the principal melodic component of the Tagunggu’ ensemble.
researchNotes: The kulintangan usually consists of seven to nine small gongs arranged in tonal order.

Although the individual gongs have no formal names, Bajau practitioners commonly group them as palinduan (two or three lower-numbered gongs, usually 1–3), paletehan or pamaletehan (usually gongs 4–7), and parindil or teng-teng (gongs 8–9).
The wooden beater used to strike the kulintangan is known as tingan.
interviewNotes: Kulintangan gongs were traditionally made from brass. Iron may now be used because brass is difficult to obtain.
Skilled makers were identified in Matunggong, Kudat, and Kota Belud.

name: Agung
description: Three large hanging gongs that reinforce the rhythmic and sonic structure of the Tagunggu’ ensemble.

detailedNotes.text: The agung produces a firm, authoritative low-frequency sound. In performance, it marks time, helps control tempo, and maintains musical continuity.
For the Bajau community, the agung forms part of langkapan—ancestral heirlooms with significant symbolic and spiritual value.
The wooden agung beater is known as tigung.
Agung gongs were traditionally made from brass, with iron also used today.

noteGroups.heading: Classification and functions of the three agung
noteGroups.intro: The smaller agung is known as agung sambut, the larger agung as agung lusung, and the flatter agung as agung bua. Each of the three has its own function.

items.text: Agung bua, also known as canang or bell, completes and strengthens the musical flow or sulimbag—the rhythmic arrangement—depending on the player’s skill.

Agung sambut is also known as agung tawag-tawag. Its name comes from the Suluk word tawag, meaning “to call”. It functions as a signal and is usually played rapidly. In the past, its strokes were used to summon the community or signal an emergency such as a death.
Agung lusung responds to or answers the musical flow or sulimbag. Agung sambut and agung lusung complement one another’s sound.

soundboardDescription: From the left: agung bua, the largest agung lusung in the centre, and the smallest agung sambut or agung tawag-tawag on the right. Press each gong to hear its recording.

name: Tambul
description: A double-headed drum that produces a repeated, consistent pulse and acts as the principal rhythmic driver of the Tagunggu’ ensemble.
researchNotes: Strong, continuous tambul strokes shape the music’s dynamics and reinforce the ensemble’s overall rhythmic structure.

Like the agung, the tambul forms part of langkapan—an ancestral heirloom with symbolic and spiritual value—and is therefore subject to customary restrictions concerning its care and playing technique.
Earlier tambul were commonly made from wood with goatskin membranes. Contemporary construction may use metals such as brass and alloy.
The wooden beater used to strike the tambul is known as tibul.
interviewNotes: Tambul uses refined goatskin heads, a wooden frame including suitable root wood, a brass or iron body, and coarse sack-like tension rope.
Hard, termite-resistant wood such as belian or ipil was used for the beater.
A drum purchased from a musical-instrument shop may be used as a substitute today.
